report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.title: Parenting Stress and Child Anxiety: Exploring Potential Moderators
table.research_questions:
Literature on parenting stress, or stress that arises from the demands of parenting, has previously shown a salient influence on children’s internalizing and externalizing behaviors (Rodriguez, 2011; Tsotsi et al., 2019). However, there remains a gap in research that would look exclusively and specifically at its influence on anxiety in childhood. We're also interested in identifying potential moderating effects of one parent and one child factor that may emerge as risk or protective factors in the strength of this relationship. 

The parent factor we plan to explore is psychological distress, or more simply, the parent’s mental health status. Multiple studies (Babore et al., 2023; Tsoti et al., 2019) found parenting stress to act as a moderator between the mental health of parent and child, therefore we’re interested to see if parent mental health and parenting stress can be swapped in this triadic relationship. As such, we expect higher parent psychological distress to strengthen the relationship between parent stress and child anxiety.

The child factor we chose to examine is child resilience. Higher levels of resilience have historically been found to act as a protective factor against developing psychopathology, and so we predict higher resilience to weaken the relationship between parenting stress and child anxiety.

Our hypotheses are as follows:
H1: Increased parenting stress will be positively associated with higher child anxiety.
H2: The positive relationship between parenting stress and child anxiety will be stronger when parents report higher levels of psychological distress.
H3: The positive relationship between parenting stress and child anxiety will be weaker when children report higher levels of resilience.
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
We will use a hierarchical linear model (HLM) to account for the nested structure of the data (i.e., children are nested within parents/families). First, we will prepare the data (i.e., examine the distributions of all the variables, center the predictors for clarity in interpreting the results, and check for missing data). Then, we will use a sequential approach for model building. We will first test the unconditional model (no predictors; estimating the intraclass correlations to examine the variance at each level). After testing the unconditional model, we will conduct three sequential multilevel models corresponding to each research question.

Research Question 1: We will use a random intercepts model with parenting stress as a Level 1 predictor of child anxiety.

Research Question 2: A cross-level interaction model, where parenting stress (Level 1), parent psychological distress (Level 2) and their interaction predict child anxiety. Parenting stress will be group-mean centered and psychological distress will be grand-mean centered to ensure that Level 2 effects are interpreted as deviations from the overall mean.

Research Question 3: We will use a Level 1 moderation model in which parenting stress (Level 1), child resilience (Level 1), and the interaction effect will be used to predict child anxiety. Group-mean centering will be used.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to analysis of the data
table.existing_data_explanation: We are using secondary data for this study, however data access has been limited with each of the coauthors. Madison Poisall accessed the raw dataset in Fall 2023 to assist with minor data cleaning. Stephanie Estrera accessed the dataset in Spring 2025 to examine the missingness rates of each measured variable (calculated by using mean(is.na(VARIABLE))) * 100) in R. Callie Little accessed the raw dataset in Fall 2023 to assist with minor data cleaning. Sara Hart has not accessed the dataset herself directly.
table.data_collection_procedures: Procedures can be found in detail in Hart et al. (2019). The following recruitment is for the larger National Project on Achievement in Twins (NatPAT) study. Elementary schools who use the Dynamic Indicators of Basic Early Literacy Skills (DIBELS) assessment were contacted and asked to pass out recruitment materials to any twins or multiples in their school. If a family agreed, they reached out to the lab directly and they were mailed questionnaires. Following the completion of the questionnaires, they were mailed back to the lab and manually entered into the REDCap software by research assistants. Once participants were enrolled in the larger study, existing NatPAT families were mailed separate consents and questionnaires that asked about their experiences during and after COVID-19 as part of another study focused on COVID-19. 567 families responded to the COVID 2023 survey that will be used in the present study.
table.sample_size: A total of 567 families and 1,134 twins will be included (one parent and two twins per family).
table.sample_size_rationale: A power analysis was conducted using G*Power (version 3.1) to determine the required sample size for detecting a moderation effect in a multiple linear regression model. Assuming a small effect size (f² = 0.02), α = .05, and power (1 – β) = .80, the required sample size was calculated to be 395 participants. However, the final sample size for this study will include approximately 567 families and 1,134 children which both exceeds the minimum power to detect small-sized effects.
table.measured_variables:
Parenting Stress:
Parents completed a one item parenting stress measure that asks “During the 2022-2023 school year, how stressful were your parenting experiences with your child?”, with responses on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Not at all) to 5 (Very much). The item is adapted from the parenting stress question from Prime et al.’s (2021) COVID-19 Family Stressor Scale.

Child Anxiety:
Children completed a truncated version of the Spence Children’s Anxiety Scale (Spence et al., 2003) to assess the severity of anxiety symptoms. 8 items were included from the original 44 and are ranked on a 4-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Never) to 4 (Always). This scale will be scored by computing sum scores, where higher scores will indicate greater levels of anxiety in the child.

Parent Psychological Distress:
Parents completed the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale, a 10-item measure asking about various domains of psychological distress on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (None of the time) to 5 (All the time). Items are from Andrews & Slade (2001) and will be scored by computing sum scores, where higher scores will indicate greater psychological distress present in the parent.


Child Resilience:
Children completed the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS; Smith et al., 2008) to measure their ability to bounce back. It is a 6 item measure ranked on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 5 (Strongly agree). This scale will be scored by computing sum scores, where higher scores will indicate higher resilience present in the child.
table.statistical_tests:
We will use a hierarchical linear model (HLM) to account for the nested structure of the data (i.e., children are nested within parents/families). First, we will prepare the data (i.e., examine the distributions of all the variables, center the predictors for clarity in interpreting the results, and check for missing data). Then, we will use a sequential approach for model building. We will first test the unconditional model (no predictors; estimating the intraclass correlations to examine the variance at each level). After testing the unconditional model, we will conduct three sequential multilevel models corresponding to each research question.

Research Question 1: We will use a random intercepts model with parenting stress as a Level 1 predictor of child anxiety.

Research Question 2: A cross-level interaction model, where parenting stress (Level 1), parent psychological distress (Level 2) and their interaction predict child anxiety. Parenting stress will be group-mean centered and psychological distress will be grand-mean centered to ensure that Level 2 effects are interpreted as deviations from the overall mean.

table.inference_criteria:
P-value: less than .05 will be reported as significant.
Standardized coefficients: we will report the standardized coefficients (i.e., grand mean or centering for interpretation ease)
Johnson-Neyman technique for probing interactions: For significant interactions, we will also conduct a Johnson-Neyman technique to probe the interaction by identifying the specific ranges of parent distress (RQ 2) and resilience (RQ 3) at which parenting stress is a significant predictor of child anxiety. We will use the johnson_neyman() function from the R package “interactions”. (Bauer & Curran, 2005)

Confidence intervals: Confidence intervals that do not include 0 will be interpreted as statistically significant.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: We will examine the descriptive statistics for all variables, and visually inspect each variable using histograms and boxplots. Cases where individual scores are smaller than the 1st quartile and larger than the 3rd quartile will be flagged as potential outliers. Potential outliers will be Winsorized (i.e., brough to the nearest interquartile fence) as a more conservative approach rather than removing whole cases. Winsorized data will be documented, and we will run sensitivity analyses to compare the results of the raw vs. Winsorized data.
table.missing_data_handling: We will first check and report missingness rates at both the case level and variable level for each of our four main variables (i.e., parenting stress, child anxiety, parent psychological distress, and child resilience). We will conduct Little’s MCAR test to assess whether data may be missing completely at random (MCAR; Little, 1988). If the test is significant (p < 0.05), likely indicating that the data are missing completely at random (MCAR), we’ll decide based on looking at the data to either proceed with mean imputation or regression imputation. If the test is non-significant (p > 0.05), likely indicating that the data are missing at random (MAR), we will proceed with multiple imputation. If we believe any cases to be missing not at random (MNAR), we will conduct sensitivity analyses to evaluate the potential impact of these cases on key findings.

text.text: Parenting stress, or stress that arises from the demands of parenting, has been linked with children's internalizing and externalizing behaviors (Rodriguez, 2011; Tsotsi et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Parenting stress, or stress that arises from the demands of parenting, has been linked with children's internalizing and externalizing behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Rodriguez, 2011;</ref> Tsotsi et al., 2019).

text.text: Of these behaviors, less is known about its unique relation to anxiety, a prevalent and significant disorder for many children.

The present study aims to address this gap by examining the relation between parenting stress and childhood anxiety while also testing whether parental psychological distress or child resilience would emerge as significant moderators.
Parenting stress was found to positively predict children's anxiety, such that as parenting stress increases, so does child anxiety.
However, neither parental psychological distress nor child resilience emerged as significant moderators of this relation.

Future studies should explore other potential variables that could act as risk or resilience factors to further our understanding of factors that may exacerbate or protect against increased child anxiety due to parenting stress.
Anxiety has been shown to affect many aspects of a child's life.

Current literature demonstrates that children with clinical anxiety disorders exhibit greater impairment in domains of the home, school, and peers as well as impairment in overall quality of life compared to their non-anxious peers (Dickson et al., 2024).

text.text: Childhood anxiety is a widely recognized and frequently studied problem and can last into adolescence or adulthood if not properly treated (Essau et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Childhood anxiety is a widely recognized and frequently studied problem and can last into adolescence or adulthood if not properly treated <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Essau et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Prior studies have credited the development of anxiety disorders in children to a number of factors, including genetic vulnerability and environmental factors (Murray et al. 2009).
text.formatted: Prior studies have credited the development of anxiety disorders in children to a number of factors, including genetic vulnerability and environmental factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Murray et al. 2009</ref>).

text.text: One such environmental factor is the parent-child relationship, which has been deemed as a salient predictor of children's developing psychopathology.
Within this work on the parentchild relationship, parenting stress, or psychological distress that arises from the demands of parenting, has been indicated as a risk factor (Deater-Deckard, 1998).
text.formatted: Within this work on the parentchild relationship, parenting stress, or psychological distress that arises from the demands of parenting, has been indicated as a risk factor <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Deater-Deckard, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: One meta-analytical review concluded that parenting stress was positively associated with children's internalizing and externalizing behaviors, poorer parent-child relationship quality, reduced parental engagement with the child, and poorer parental mental health during the COVID-19 pandemic (Chung et al., 2024).
text.formatted: One meta-analytical review concluded that parenting stress was positively associated with children's internalizing and externalizing behaviors, poorer parent-child relationship quality, reduced parental engagement with the child, and poorer parental mental health during the COVID-19 pandemic <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chung et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The literature consistently identifies this domain-specific stress as an influence on the development of both internalizing and externalizing disorders in children (Rodriguez, 2011; Tsotsi et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The literature consistently identifies this domain-specific stress as an influence on the development of both internalizing and externalizing disorders in children <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Rodriguez, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Tsotsi et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: As parenting stress is relatively common, the extent to which it can impact children's outcomes is likely to be of particular interest to parents who experience it.

Moreover, because parent-child interactions and their subsequent impacts on children's development are complex and likely the culmination of a variety of factors, we seek to explore other commonly studied relevant factors that may impact parenting stress' influence.
Much of the existing literature on parenting stress and its influence on children links increased parenting stress with child externalizing behaviors (Tsoti et al., 2019b; Solem et al., 2011).

text.text: A certain level of parenting stress is expected and considered normal.
Increased parenting stress, however, has been found to be associated with children's behavioral issues (Williford et al., 2007; Mak et al., 2020).

text.text: This finding aligns with a transactional model, such that children's development is influenced by continuous, reciprocal interactions between the child and aspects of their environment (Sameroff & Mackenzie, 2003), in this case, the parenting they receive.

Applying this risk and resilience framework to consider variables that can change the strength and or direction of the relation between parenting stress and child anxiety would further our understanding of the mechanisms at play as well as inform future research and intervention work.

Psychological distress, or the discomforting emotional state experienced by an individual in response to a specific stressor (Ridner, 2004), may commonly act as a deterrent to normal daily functioning.

text.text: These studies demonstrate how these three variables can interact, with parenting stress commonly being found as a mechanism through which parental distress influences children's mental health.

Because parental distress has been shown to have the power to influence children's mental health on its own, in addition to the culminating risk from both parental stress and distress, we were interested in examining whether it had such power to change the strength of the relation between parenting stress and child anxiety.
Resilience is a commonly studied protective factor in children, with much of the prior research examining it as a moderator of the association between other variables.

For example, one study found that resilience moderated the relation between COVID-19's psychological impact and anxiety symptoms in adolescents, such that those with higher resilience showed fewer anxiety symptoms in relation to COVID-19 than those with lower resilience (Traunmüller et al., 2023).

text.text: Another study found that resilience moderated the relation between number of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and odds of having mental health disorders, with children having higher resilience exhibiting lower odds of having mental health disorders in relation to their number of ACEs as compared to children with lower resilience (Okwori, 2022).

text.text: Some studies have found resilience to have a moderating effect on the relation between stress and the mental health of either the child (Anyan & Hjemdal, 2016) or the parent (Wu et al., 2025), however, it remains to be seen if resilience will appear to alter the impact of parenting stress in particular.

text.text: As these findings point to resilience being a robust protective factor against mental health risks in increased risk individuals, it is unknown how it may mitigate the impact of parenting stress on anxiety symptoms.
Our research questions are as follows: 1) is parenting stress associated with children's anxiety?
2) Does parental psychological distress moderate this relation?
3) Does children's resilience moderate this relation?
We predict that we'll find a statistically significant positive relation between parenting stress and child anxiety.

Moreover, as we examine both parental psychological distress and child resilience as moderators of the association between parenting stress and child anxiety, we hypothesize that parental psychological distress will strengthen the influence of parenting stress on child anxiety and increased resilience in the child will weaken the relation between parenting stress and child anxiety.

text.text: The NatPAT project sought to examine twin's academic achievement and researchers partnered with the University of Oregon to use their Dynamic Indicators of Basic Early Literacy Skills (DIBELS) database of participating schools.

Beginning in 2021, NatPAT participants were invited to be part of a new project focused on caregivers' and twins' experiences following the COVID-19 pandemic and the impacts on their personal and educational lives.
This COVID-19 focused project uses a cohort sequential design with annual surveys sent to families for one caregiver and both twins (if enrolled in, or having completed, grade 3) to complete.

The present study will use the 2023 wave of survey data collection that asked parents and twins about their COVID-related and general experiences during the 2022-2023 school year, as well as mental health related measures relevant to our research questions.
For this study, participants included 576 caregivers and 1,152 children.
Children were nearly equally distributed in sex (male: 48.2%, N = 555; female: 51.8%, N = 597) and parents were mostly biological mothers (85.8%, N = 494).

In regard to race, twins identified as White (87.1%, N = 1006), Mixed race (6%, N = 68), Black or African American (4.8%, N = 54), Asian (0.7%, N = 8), American Indian/Alaska Native (0.5%, N = 6), and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (0.2%, N = 2).
Moreover, 91% (N = 1048) identified as non-Hispanic/Latino.
Families lived across the geographical United States, with survey responses from families across 40 states.
Children's ages ranged from 8 to 17 years old (M = 13.2, SD = 2.21).
The 2023 wave survey was sent to all families who were currently enrolled in the project with children under the age of 18.
Parents were asked questions about themselves and each of their twins or multiples, receiving a $50 gift card for the completion and return of this questionnaire.
Children were asked questions about themselves and were given a $20 gift card for the completion and return of their questionnaires.

Parents completed a one item parenting stress measure that asks, "During the 2021-2022 school year, how stressful were your parenting experiences with your child?", with responses on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Not at all) to 5 (Very much).

To address our first research question, we conducted a random intercepts model with parenting stress as a Level 1 predictor of child anxiety.

The current study sought to investigate the relation between parenting stress and children's anxiety, while also exploring whether parental psychological distress and child resilience would emerge as moderators.
Our results revealed a significant main effect between parenting stress and child anxiety, both confirming our hypothesis and mirroring prior literature.

Similar to how past research has found parenting stress to be associated with internalizing symptomology in children (e.g., Rodriquez, 2011) and with children's anxiety in particular (e.g., van Oort et al., 2010), we found that as parenting stress increased, so did child anxiety.
text.formatted: Similar to how past research has found parenting stress to be associated with internalizing symptomology in children (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Rodriquez, 2011)</ref> and with children's anxiety in particular (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">van Oort et al., 2010)</ref>, we found that as parenting stress increased, so did child anxiety.

text.text: This finding lends itself to further the conversation of the unique role of parenting stress in the etiology of children's anxiety.

While past research has considered factors such as parenting styles and behaviors, future studies should investigate potential parental mechanisms through which parenting stress may be influencing child anxiety.
Nevertheless, our result adds to the validity of the relation of these two variables and leads us to consider what factors may hinder or exacerbate their influence.

Beyond the direct association between parent stress and child anxiety, we were interested in examining whether parental psychological distress or child resilience would play a moderating role in the relation between parenting stress and child anxiety.

Past research supports that parenting stress mediates the relation between parental distress and child anxiety (Tsoti et al., 2019; Babore et al., 2023), and we wondered if it would extend as a moderator as laid out by the cumulative risk framework (Appleyard et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Past research supports that parenting stress mediates the relation between parental distress and child anxiety <ref type="bibr">(Tsoti et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Babore et al., 2023)</ref>, and we wondered if it would extend as a moderator as laid out by the cumulative risk framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Appleyard et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Parent psychological distress was a statistically significant main effect on child anxiety.
However, our results did not support parent distress as a moderator, which suggests that it may be limited to the mediating pathway as described in prior work.
The cumulative risk framework did not appear to apply to this sample in the way we hypothesized.

Further confirming the well-known protective effects of increased resilience in children (Traunmüller et al., 2023), we found that child resilience demonstrated statistically significant main effects and predicted decreased anxiety in our sample.
text.formatted: Further confirming the well-known protective effects of increased resilience in children <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Traunmüller et al., 2023</ref>), we found that child resilience demonstrated statistically significant main effects and predicted decreased anxiety in our sample.

text.text: Additionally, we hypothesized that resilience would buffer the impact of parenting stress on child anxiety, similar to previous reports (e.g., Anyan & Hjemdal, 2016; Wu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Additionally, we hypothesized that resilience would buffer the impact of parenting stress on child anxiety, similar to previous reports (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Anyan & Hjemdal, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Wu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Although it demonstrated an association with decreased child anxiety, there was not a statistically significant interaction between parenting stress and child resilience.

In total, neither parent psychological distress nor child resilience emerged as statistically significant moderators, suggesting that although they are each correlated with child anxiety, they are not interactive on the relation between parent stress and child anxiety.
While this was contrary to our initial hypotheses, these results still inform our understanding of the relation between these oft-associated variables.

Agreeing with the current literature, parents experiencing increased distress may contribute to their child's own anxiety symptoms and children with increased resilience may experience protective effects against potential parental influences leading to anxiety.

However, while these variables independently contribute to children's anxiety, from our findings it does not appear that they interact in a way that supports a risk and resilience framework being applied to this specific combination of variables.
While our results add to established literature on additive pathways to children's anxiety, there are several limitations to consider.
One limitation may be the brevity of the parenting stress measure.
Because it is a one-item scale, it's possible it lacks the intricacies that could provide a more thorough look at the concept of parenting stress.
Similarly, as this measure is self-report and given the subject, has the potential for social desirability bias.
Future studies may wish to use a more comprehensive measure or collect biological data to get a fuller and unbiased picture of parenting stress.

Another limitation may lie in the substantial unexplained variance in each of the models, indicating there are other factors not measured in the present study that further explain between-family differences in child anxiety.

Including a wider range of familial factors in future models may help account for more of this variance as well as identify additional risk or resilience factors that may prove statistically significant in protecting against or exacerbating children's anxiety from parenting stress.

Because parenting stress is widely prevalent and shown to interact with children's anxiety, future research should explore how best to identify afflicted families and examine best practices and interventions to mitigate parental effects on children's mental health.
Our sample had generally low levels of symptomology overall and future researchers may want to apply this methodology to more clinical samples to determine if the effects still hold.

In sum, our findings provide a foundation for researchers to clarify family-level factors underlying the etiology of anxiety in children, consider child-specific interventions, and provide parents with actionable insights into supporting their children's mental well-being.
